facts.text: Nuisance braking is an automatic brake application that was not needed because there was no real object (a false intervention) or because a real object posed no danger (an unnecessary intervention).
facts.quote: Nuisance braking is an automatic brake application that was not needed, either because there was no real object (a false intervention) or because the object was real but posed no danger (an unnecessary intervention).

facts.text: The booklet adapts nuisance-braking vocabulary from a NIOSH field study of a radar warning system on a haul truck.
facts.quote: The vocabulary comes from a NIOSH field study of a radar warning system on a haul truck, and the booklet carries its definitions over to braking [Chapter 4].

facts.text: In the NIOSH haul-truck study's vocabulary, false alarms report insignificant objects such as ruts, rocks, bushes or the truck's own tires; nuisance alarms correctly detect an object but indicate no urgent danger because the operator knows about the object and the task requires approaching it.
facts.quote: A *nuisance* alarm is technically correct, the object is there, but there is no urgent danger because the operator knows about it and the task requires the approach

facts.text: Backing a haul truck toward a rock pile to be loaded is an example of a task-required approach that can produce a nuisance alarm.
facts.quote: for example backing toward a rock pile to be loaded.

facts.text: In the NIOSH haul-truck radar-warning field study, 18% of alarms were false, 42% were nuisance and 40% warranted action.
facts.quote: In that study 18% of alarms were false, 42% were nuisance and 40% warranted action [Chapter 4].

facts.text: False and nuisance alarm categories produce nuisance braking when they trigger brakes rather than a buzzer.
facts.quote: Nuisance braking is what happens when the first two categories drive the brakes instead of a buzzer.

facts.text: Underground stop-capable proximity systems unnecessarily shut down vehicles at frequencies ranging from once a day to 15 times during a single cut of coal.
facts.quote: Underground, stop-capable proximity systems "unnecessarily shut down vehicles anywhere from once a day up to 15 times during a single cut of coal"

facts.text: Workers using underground stop-capable proximity systems reported jarring and jolting stops.
facts.quote: workers reported jarring and jolting stops

facts.text: A manufacturer reported 5–10% production loss while underground proximity detection was active, although two mine operators said production recovered.
facts.quote: a manufacturer reported 5 to 10% production loss while proximity detection was active, although two mine operators said production recovered [Chapter 4].

facts.text: The booklet identifies a chain from unnecessary interventions to annoyance, lost production and new hazards, then to bypass, override, tag removal and widened zones, ultimately losing protection when needed.
facts.quote: runs from unnecessary interventions to annoyance, lost production and new hazards, then to bypass, override, tag removal and widened zones, and finally to protection being lost when it is needed [Chapter 4].

facts.text: The booklet identifies nuisance interventions as the main documented field failure of deployed proximity systems.
facts.quote: Chapter 8 calls nuisance interventions the main documented field failure of deployed proximity systems [Chapter 8].

facts.text: Improving the sensor alone does not resolve nuisance braking: most unwanted alarms in the haul-truck study were nuisance rather than false, requiring understanding of the task, intention and object type.
facts.quote: A better sensor alone does not fix it. In the haul-truck study most unwanted alarms were nuisance, not false, so the task, the intention and the kind of object had to be understood [Chapter 4].

facts.text: Nuisance braking cannot be measured on a test track with staged targets; measurement requires real operations and task-specific rates per operating hour, loading cycle and reverse maneuver.
facts.quote: Nor can it be measured on a test track with staged targets; it needs real operations, measured as unnecessary interventions per operating hour, per loading cycle and per reverse maneuver, by task [Chapter 4].

facts.text: The booklet recommends running new software in shadow mode on fielded machines, computing but not executing brake commands, to measure the nuisance-brake rate before enabling braking.
facts.quote: run the new software in shadow mode (computing but not executing brake commands) on fielded machines so the nuisance-brake rate is measured before braking is enabled [Chapter 1]

facts.text: The booklet recommends making nuisance-intervention rate an acceptance metric with equal weight to missed interventions.
facts.quote: make the nuisance-intervention rate an acceptance metric equal in weight to missed interventions [Chapter 8].

facts.text: The relative tuning cost of a nuisance brake versus a missed intervention is a safety-policy decision that should be documented rather than hidden in a formula.
facts.quote: How much a nuisance brake should "cost" relative to a miss when tuning is a safety-policy decision to be written down, not hidden in a formula [Chapter 9].

facts.text: The booklet identifies nuisance braking as the most likely CMS service failure: machines stop so often that people switch off the system, rather than the system simply missing a hazard.
facts.quote: Nuisance braking is the most likely way for the CMS to fail in service: not by missing a hazard, but by stopping machines so often that people switch it off [Chapters 4, 8].

facts.text: The manufacturer's experience that balancing detection against false positives took years is the reason for the virtual-validation program.
facts.quote: The manufacturer's own experience that balancing detection against false positives took years is the reason the program exists [Introduction].
